opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the first thing I'd say is that we try not to let the roadmap be driven by what everyone else is doing. It's very easy in this field to get reactive, to see a strong release from another lab and feel like you have to chase that particular benchmark or that particular feature. That's usually a trap. If you're always responding, you're always a step behind.

What we try to do instead is keep a pretty clear view of the handful of bets we think really matter over the next few years, and then ask whether the progress happening around us changes those bets. Sometimes it does. If the whole field shows that some technique works really well, you'd be foolish to ignore it, and you fold that into how you think. But most of the time what you learn is about execution, not direction.

The other thing is that a field that's improving quickly is actually good news for research. It means the baseline keeps rising, so the questions you can ask get more interesting. Things that seemed out of reach a couple of years ago, like models doing long chains of reasoning, working on problems for extended stretches, or contributing to research themselves, are now things you can actually go after. So the roadmap shouldn't just say "make the current thing better." It should be about reaching for the capabilities that weren't feasible before.

And then there's a balance between exploration and exploitation. As things mature you naturally get pressure to put more resources into scaling what already works, and that matters. But I think it's really important to protect a meaningful chunk of compute and people for exploratory work, the ideas that might not pan out. Historically a lot of the biggest jumps came from bets that looked a little uncertain at the start. If you lose that, you might stay competitive for a while, but you stop being the place where the next paradigm comes from.

So in short: stay grounded in a long-term thesis, be honest when the evidence says you should update, and keep investing in the risky stuff even when the near-term competition is intense.

r001.rationale: The response says to keep a clear set of long-term research bets and that new progress usually informs execution rather than direction, while allowing for evidence-based updates.

r002.rationale: The response discusses balancing compute between scaling and exploratory work, but does not identify compute-allocation decisions as checkpoints for reassessing whether compute supports the highest-priority bets.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's something we think about constantly, because the ground really is shifting under us.

I'd say the first thing is that we have to stay honest about where the frontier actually is. A few years ago, the gap between what we could do and what anyone else could do was pretty wide, and that gave you a lot of room to just pursue the things you found interesting. Now there are a lot of very strong labs, open-weight models have gotten really good, and the time between a capability showing up in one place and showing up everywhere has collapsed to months. So you can't build a roadmap around the assumption that you'll be alone in some capability for very long. You have to build it around being the first to get to the next thing, and also around what you do once you get there.

The second thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is that the models themselves are becoming part of the research process. A lot of our researchers now spend their time directing models to run experiments, write infrastructure, sweep hyperparameters, debug training runs. That changes what a research org looks like. The bottleneck shifts from "how many brilliant people can I put on this" to "how good is my taste about which problems matter, and how fast can I turn ideas into experiments." So part of the roadmap has to be investing in our own tooling, in making our researchers more leveraged, because that compounds.

Third, I'd say we have to stay disciplined about the things that are hard to copy. Raw benchmark performance gets commoditized quickly. What's harder is the deep stuff: reasoning that generalizes to problems you haven't seen, reliability over long horizons, models that can actually act in the world and recover from mistakes, and the safety and alignment work that lets you deploy all of that responsibly. Those are long-term bets, and I think they're where the real differentiation is going to come from. We shouldn't be dragged into just chasing whatever leaderboard is hot this week.

And then the last piece is culture. The reason OpenAI has gotten where it has is that people were willing to make big, somewhat contrarian bets, like scaling, like reinforcement learning on reasoning, before those were obvious. As the field matures and gets more competitive, the pressure is to get more incremental and more defensive. I think the right adaptation is actually the opposite. You want to keep a core of the org that's protected from the near-term roadmap and is just asking "what's the thing that, if it worked, would change everything?" Because that's what got us here, and it's the only thing that keeps you ahead when everyone else is also really good.

r001.rationale: The response recommends adapting the roadmap to the changing field, but does not say the high-level roadmap should remain more stable than implementation details.

r002.rationale: The response discusses investing in research tooling and protecting long-term bets, but does not identify compute-allocation decisions as checkpoints for reviewing whether compute serves the highest-priority bets.

astra-6.text:
I think the roadmap has to stay flexible. As models improve across the field, you have to keep asking: what are the bottlenecks now, and which research directions could actually change what these systems can do?

It helps to distinguish between improvements you expect from continuing on the current trajectory and problems that need a new idea. You want to keep making progress on the first, while leaving enough room to explore the second. Otherwise, you can get very good at optimizing something that’s no longer the most important constraint.

And capability isn’t the whole story. If a model gets much better at solving a problem, but people still can’t reliably use it, that gap becomes a research priority. So I’d want the roadmap to respond to what we’re learning from both the research and actual use, while keeping a longer-term focus on reliability and safety.

r001.rationale: The response says the roadmap should stay flexible as models improve, but does not distinguish stable high-level priorities from changing implementation details.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention compute allocation or reassessing whether compute supports the highest-priority research bets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want a strong point of view, but you also have to be willing to update it. As models improve, the bottlenecks change. Something that looked like a fundamental limitation six months ago might suddenly become an engineering problem, and that should affect where you put your research effort.

So I’d separate the long-term direction from the specific bets. The direction is building more capable, reliable, useful systems. The bets—what to scale, which learning signals to use, how much to invest in a particular approach—should respond to evidence. You need room for researchers to try things that don’t fit the current recipe, while also having the discipline to scale up the things that actually work.

And I think using the models is a big part of that feedback loop. Benchmarks tell you something, but watching where a model falls short on a real task often gives you a much clearer sense of what the next research problem should be.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a steady long-term direction from specific bets that should change as evidence and model capabilities evolve.

r002.rationale: It mentions choices about what to scale and how much to invest, but does not identify compute allocation as a checkpoint for reassessing whether compute supports the highest-priority bets.
